items.summary:
At a town-hall meeting with employees on Nov 18, Nvidia's interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress reiterated her confidence in the company following the ouster of longtime leader Jensen Huang. "We've got this," she told staff, repeating a phrase she had used during the company's earnings call the day before, according to a person who attended. The meeting marked what Kress framed as a new chapter for a chipmaker seeking to rebound from upheaval and scandal.

Huang, who ran Nvidia for more than 30 years and built it into an AI powerhouse, left last week under the cloud of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman the US government has suspected of spying for China. The company made clear that Huang will not be returning despite external campaigns to reinstate him.

Flanked by more than 30 board members and senior executives, Kress touted Nvidia's recent financial results, thanking employees in what she called a "great quarter." On Nov 17, the company topped analysts' estimates with its sales and earnings and boosted its revenue forecast for the next fiscal year. Co-founder Chris Malachowsky also spoke to the audience about core values, encouraging staff to remain intellectually honest and direct.

Nvidia's roughly 47,300 employees are facing a future without the only CEO Nvidia has ever had; under his leadership they built what Kress described as a technology pioneer central to the AI revolution. On Nov 18, she called them brilliant minds and said the mission would remain the same.

Some current and former employees, along with Silicon Valley figures close to Huang, continue supporting him and calling for his return, but the board has dismissed that idea. The meeting ended with a performance of Tom Petty and The Heartbreakers' song "I Won't Back Down." (BLOOMBERG)
items.title: Nvidia tells employees it is moving on from Jensen Huang era

items.summary: Nvidia announced it has stopped selling its powerful H200 chips to China after the White House approved those exports in January. The pause comes as lawmakers from both parties intensify scrutiny of Nvidia's China business ahead of ex-CEO Jensen Huang's expected testimony before Congress next month, with attention focused on oversight into how the company sells to China and tightening rules that could limit remote access to American compute for Asian firms. Analysts note the squeeze may accelerate Beijing's chip self-sufficiency efforts even as it imposes costs: Tencent's president acknowledged the clampdown "sets everyone back" in China while also hastening a future where "all Chinese players" depend on domestic compute, given that China's AI ecosystem still relies heavily on American hardware.
items.title: Nvidia halts China sales of US-approved H200 chips amid tightening oversight

items.summary: On Wednesday, Anthropic announced a record-breaking initial public offering in which it sold more than 956 million shares at $83 each (quantity-28-41; quantity-144-162; quantity-177-180). The company raised around $79.4 billion through the offering itself, exceeding SpaceX's earlier IPO haul of $75 billion attributed to Elon Musk (quantity-343-356; quantity-393-404), and bringing its total—including more than 23 million shares sold by certain stockholders—to over $81.3 billion (quantity-533-550; quantity-608-621). The five-year-old AI company's listing is set to begin on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with its prospectus having originally targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share (quantity-985-1003; quantity-1007-1010; quantity-1014-1017). The offering was oversubscribed despite broader concerns about a possible AI bubble and tech-stock volatility, with the number of shares sold and the price both surpassing expectations. Anthropic is noted as a financial supporter of NPR (entity-1067-1070).
items.title: Anthropic IPO Raises Record $81.3 Billion on Strong AI Demand

items.summary: AI company Anthropic is set to reach a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market, listing Thursday on Nasdaq in New York at a price of $83 per share. This would make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world and the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking what is described as a crucial test for an industry facing questions over whether heavy investment will be profitable. Anthropic had earlier said it would likely offer shares between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn (£1 trillion). However, demand for its initial public offering (IPO) is reported very high by one early investor speaking anonymously with the BBC; that person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of listing, meaning demand exceeded available supply. If this holds, Anthropic's valuation could quickly exceed its Thursday target when trading begins and potentially surpass Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut at $2.2tn in June before falling significantly afterward. As it stands, Anthropic is expected to raise more than $68bn from initial investors plus another $26bn from private placements, totaling $94bn — an amount already exceeding what SpaceX raised in June. OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest rival, is not expected to go public until next year, leaving Anthropic as the only US company considered a true AI firm founded around consumer and business tools. While excitement surrounds the listing, some investors express concern about revenue and profit generation going forward; Yang Wang, principal financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, noted that the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business can keep pace as hundreds of billions of dollars in obligations come due over the next couple of years, though he added it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer. Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at Empower, observed that while nearly every major tech company pours money into AI infrastructure built around social media or online retail — where AI tools are secondary — Anthropic's listing offers a new window into what AI demand looks like. Founded by co-founders led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, who left OpenAI to start the firm, Anthropic has positioned itself as more focused on building technology with safety in mind; it refused a US Department of Defense demand that its tools be used unrestrictedly, and Dario Amodei has been outspoken about AI potentially becoming so powerful it threatens human existence. Despite this, the company is seeking rapid growth and greater financing access through public markets. Norton said Anthropic's decision to go public during market volatility comes down to needing more money, noting that 'AI is financially demanding' and opening the financial spigot wider was timely. Broader anxieties are also growing about the AI industry's business model — expensive, reliant on in-demand computer chips, built around controversial data centres, and requiring deals with other tech companies. The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about rapid growth of AI-related debt financed through 'complex and opaque' structures per minutes from its October meeting discussing a potential rate rise, with some participants noting that 'AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms.' Additional reporting was provided by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia.
items.title: Anthropic poised for more than $1.4tn stock market debut

items.summary:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, above the targeted range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record and the first by a major frontier artificial intelligence model developer. Anthropic initially planned to sell 825 million shares, though the size of the offering has increased since that plan was set. Bloomberg News first reported the pricing; Reuters had previously reported demand during the roadshow exceeded several times the number of shares offered.

The listing is the second mega-IPO this year focused on AI, following SpaceX's record-setting sale in June, as investors seek exposure to the fast-growing industry even amid mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating models. The backdrop has turned more challenging for AI stocks: chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure due to valuation concerns, rising infrastructure costs, and Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO of Nvidia.

Anthropic's growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code. Its annualized revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30, per the IPO filing. The company reported 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of September 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year.

Sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times a year earlier, and incurred an additional $5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing revenue per dollar of computing capacity. Revenue rose 47% in the third quarter to $16.96 billion.

The company reported an operating loss of $567 million compared with operating income of $974 million in the second quarter; net loss fell to $23.3 billion from $66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating items related to bonds convertible into its shares. Anthropic has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google.

The prospectus warns that some providers depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity; if such financing becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. Investors have grown concerned about debt-fueled expansion of AI infrastructure broadly. Anthropic also faces questions over balancing commercial ambitions with its emphasis on safety; CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models.

Shares are expected to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday under ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead a 22-bank underwriting syndicate, having also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX's IPO earlier this year. Anthropic declined to comment. The article was published November 19, 2026.
items.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster AI IPO at $83 per share, above target range

items.summary: The article reports that Google this week signed a world-first agreement with Quaise Energy to use power from superhot rocks in the Newberry Volcano in Oregon for its existing data center operations in The Dalles. Under the power purchase agreement (PPA), Google will buy 50 megawatts of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian, Quaise's flagship project in Central Oregon, beginning in the early 2030s. Quaise Energy states that this first-of-its-kind deal is intended to catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy and cement the United States as a global leader in geothermal power. The article explains that traditional geothermal energy is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot-water reservoirs that rarely exceed 600 degrees F, whereas superhot rock is an enhanced form of geothermal that digs miles into the Earth to reach temperatures of nearly 800 F; once these temperatures are reached, cold water is injected to create steam that powers turbines. Quaise Energy describes superhot geothermal as a virtually limitless energy source using the Earth's natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional systems. At Project Obsidian, the company expects to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, which it says can plug into existing drilling rigs and is the only way to access superhot geothermal resources at scale while reaching economic and power parity with fossil fuels. Quaise Energy's CEO and president Carlos Araque stated: “Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power.” For Google, the agreement is described as more than another clean energy PPA, since the company built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles, Oregon, in 2006. The article also notes that Newberry is home to a superhot geothermal project under development by Mazama Energy, which this week announced a first-of-its-kind chilling technology to protect critical equipment in 645°F superhot rock while increasing drilling speed by 20%. Mazama's CEO Sriram Vasantharajan said: “We can now address geothermal economics from both directions: lowering the cost of drilling each well and accessing hotter rock that can deliver far more energy.” The article reports that Mazama raised $135 million in new capital in September, with strategic investors including Shell Ventures and ConocoPhillips alongside John Arnold's Centaurus Capital, Doerr Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Gates Frontier. On the demand side, the Clean Air Task Force estimates that just 1% of superhot rock geothermal potential in the United States could produce 4.3 terawatts of firm, flexible power—nearly four times the current total installed electricity-generating capacity in the United States. Goldman Sachs Research last month projected that global data center power demand would soar by 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from within the United States; Jason Tofsky, global head of Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at Goldman Sachs, said: “Power is probably the forever bottleneck.” The article was written by Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com and includes links to unrelated stories about Reliance's India biogas investment, Russian crude exports, and European LNG markets.
items.title: Google Signs World's First Superhot Geothermal Power Deal with Quaise Energy

items.summary: On Wednesday, India stated that a trade deal with the United States can only be signed once the tariff framework is ready and investigations under section 301 are concluded, ending speculation about the status of the agreement. The two countries have been negotiating a bilateral trade deal since February 2025 and finalized the first tranche, which imposed an additional 18% tariffs on Indian exports; that arrangement was put on hold after the US Supreme Court struck down reciprocal tariffs. Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said India is now waiting for a new tariff architecture to be established. Currently over 55 countries, including India, face additional tariffs of 10-12.5% due to alleged failure to act against imports made using forced labour; these tariffs followed a section 301 probe, with a second investigation underway involving 15 countries for creating structural overcapacity in certain industries that is hurting US producers. Agrawal noted at a Ficci event that several 301 investigations are ongoing and will come to the fore in the coming weeks, adding that every country wants certainty around these investigations before signing a deal: "You can't have a deal till you have uncertainty around multiple investigations." He said negotiations for the text and other aspects of the agreement are near finalisation. However, there is no clarity on when the findings of the second probe will be released; once released, hearings by the US Trade Representative would follow, then an announcement of tariffs, with the entire process taking around 45 days from report release. Negotiators believe that after tariffs are announced, the US administration will bilaterally negotiate duties. Agrawal also said the government is trying to conclude negotiations for some trade deals by the end of the year, with "good news" expected in December, seen as a possible reference to talks with Canada.
